headline: The Fed's watchdog clears Powell. The bill still doubled.
summary: The Fed's inspector general found no grounds to believe Jerome Powell or the Fed broke a federal law on the headquarters renovation, a report said Wednesday. The Justice Department opened a criminal probe of the then chair in January and closed it in April. The report faults the Fed's management: costs more than doubled, to $2.5 billion.
cover_answer: No crime, says the watchdog. But the bill doubled.
table_question: You went way over budget but broke no rule. Are you in trouble?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The grown-ups who look after America's money are fixing up their big office. It cost more than twice the plan, like a lemonade stand meant to cost five dollars that cost twelve. Some people thought the boss cheated, so a checker looked. Nobody cheated, they just spent too much, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: The checker saying nobody cheated is the one picture a six-year-old keeps.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them and keeps one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script hands them the checker who looked and found nobody cheated. The lemonade stand carries the overspend; the billions mean nothing at this age. Expect "is the boss in trouble?" No. The checker said he broke no rule.

8-12.script: The Fed is fixing up its headquarters, and the cost doubled to $2.5 billion. Trump challenged its chair, Jerome Powell, and the Justice Department opened a criminal case in January. The Fed's own inspector general, a referee inside the building, found no crime. It did find a team that let the price climb.
8-12.why: Overspend, accusation, referee, verdict: a chain with a rule they know.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and whether rules hold for everyone, so the script hands them the chain: the cost doubled, the president challenged Powell, prosecutors opened a case, the referee checked. The verdict splits in two, no crime and bad management, a fairness call. Expect "so who pays?" The articles don't say.

13-17.script: If an investigation finds no crime, was it worth running? Prosecutors opened a criminal case into Jerome Powell in January. Wednesday the Fed's watchdog said no law was broken. Powell called it pressure over rates. Second: the Fed still let the cost double. Is no crime the same as no problem?
13-17.why: Two true things at once: cleared, and faulted.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things, and this report is two: no crime, and a project the Fed let run to twice its budget. The script gives them both, then the harder question, whether a case that ends in nothing was still pressure. Expect "was Trump right about the cost?" Partly. The marble wasn't the problem. The contracts were.

5-7.q: Did the money boss get in trouble?
5-7.a: No. A checker looked and said he broke no rule. It just cost more.

8-12.a: No. No crime, the report says. The Fed just let the cost climb.
A watchdog inside a government office who checks it follows the rules.

13-17.q: Why did Trump go after Powell?
13-17.a: The building's cost, in 2025. Powell called the probe pressure.

13-17.q: Why did it cost so much?
13-17.a: Two contracts tripled to $539 million. Not the marble.

caption:
No crime, says the watchdog. But the bill doubled.

The Fed's inspector general found no grounds to believe Jerome Powell or the Fed broke a federal law on the headquarters renovation, a report said Wednesday. The Justice Department opened a criminal probe of the then chair in January and closed it in April. The report faults the Fed's management: costs more than doubled, to $2.5 billion.

Source: Axios

Swipe for what to say at age 6, at 9, and at 17.
